messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: discrete parameters in Stan
parts:
I also wanted to briefly respond to David’s comment, “Also, seems you should extend Stan to deal with discrete parameters — usually this is simple using vanilla Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs mixed in with your HMC."

We are planning at some point to extend Stan to discrete parameters using slice sampling.  One reason we haven’t done this is that it requires some tinkering with the language itself:
1.  Stan needs to be “told” to treat discrete variables differently
2.  We need to specify the log-posterior in some way so that, when updating the discrete variables, Stan doesn’t have to compute the entire log posterior at each step.

These are doable (if necessary, we can do step 2 above in a clunky but effective way requiring some duplication of code).  We haven’t done it yet, partly because of our usual resource constraints (notably, Bob and Daniel’s time!) and partly because most of the discrete-parameter applications we’ve seen so far are finite mixture models which can be better solved by marginalizing out in the model (as described in the Stan manual).  To this end we’re also planning at some time to introduce a general mixture() distribution which will allow these models to be specified more easily and directly by users.

A

On Jul 17, 2014, at 10:35 PM, David Dunson <dun...@duke.edu> wrote:

sure -- I wonder perhaps if Stan can deal with the non-discrete mixture approach we proposed in the enclosed manuscript (to appear Biometrika).  This model is really quite simple - Gaussian process regression in a latent variable & can be trivially applied to nonparametric modeling of a random effect distribution with no discrete parameters.  Seems Stan should be good with it?  Also, seems you should extend Stan to deal with discrete parameters -- usually this is simple using vanilla Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs mixed in with your HMC.

David 

<biometrika revision5.pdf>

On Jul 17, 2014, at 12:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

I defer to David when it comes to this sort of model, so maybe the DP mixture is just fine.

Regarding Stan and HMC:  just about all existing methods (with the possible exception of the new idea of thermodynamic sampling that Mike Betancourt is working on) have problems with multimodal posteriors.  I don’t know that HMC is worse than Gibbs and Metropolis here.  The thing that HMC (and Stan) can’t handle is inference for discrete parameters.  Maybe you could do the DP mixture without discrete parameters by having a fixed number of mixture components (maybe 3 or 4) and going from there.

I’ll post this discussion the stan-users list if youall don’t object.
A

On Jul 17, 2014, at 5:04 PM, David Dunson <dun...@duke.edu> wrote:

Hi Andrew, 

I'd disagree - I think the DP mixture is really actually very simple & effectively behaves like a finite mixture.  In fact, one way to implement a good approximation to a DP mixture is to define a finite mixture with a symmetric Dirichlet prior for the mixture weights having parameters \alpha/k with k a fixed number of mixture components treated as an upper bound on the number of components needed.  This type of prior will have the effect of zeroing out the extra unnecessary components & converges to a DP as k increases.  It's a simple Gibbs sampler to implement but I don't know anything about Stan -- seemingly Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is poor for multimodal and mixture models so may fail.  Some details on such things in BDA3.

David 

On Jul 17, 2014, at 9:07 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Sure, but if you don’t have enough priror info to control a finite mixture, it seems a bit ambitoius to try to get a Dirchlet process going?

On Jul 17, 2014, at 7:42 AM, Avi Feller <avi.f...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Andy and David,

Thanks for the response. 

We've definitely thought about a mixture prior here---my guess at the "true" distribution of effects is that it's unimodal, with some heavy tails and possibly some skew. A mixture model with a small number of components could pick up some of this. While not the ideal solution, you're right that we could fit it in Stan, which is a definite plus. On the negative side, since we don't have any good prior information on mixture means (like what you did in the 1990 paper), I'm a bit wary of the mixture modeling approach here. Hence, thinking about DP priors.

All that said, you're probably right that the DP prior is overkill. But figured it was worth asking!

Great to get your thoughts, as always.

- Avi


On Wed, Jul 16, 2014 at 1:36 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
Hi, Avi.  I have an annoying habit of kicking all nonparametric questions to my coauthors…  In any case, I’m cc-ing David Dunson here.  David:  what do you think?
My general impression is that I like DP priors in some settings but it seems to me a bit of overkill to try to use them for modeling a batch of varying coefficients.  What about something simpler like a mixture model (as in my 1990 paper with King)?  That would also have the advantage of being easily fittable in Stan.
A


On Jul 15, 2014, at 7:54 AM, Avi Feller <avi.f...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Andy,

I hope that you're doing well---it's been ages since we last spoke.

I'm writing in the hope that you'll offer some useful advice on a multilevel modeling problem before I get myself in too deep. The data come from a large evaluation of Head Start, in which 3 and 4 year-old children on a wait list were randomly offered slots in Head Start, with randomization conducted separately across roughly 350 separate Head Start centers. It is of substantive interest to estimate both center-specific treatment effects and the overall distribution of those effects. Moreover, these centers are very small (many with only 2 kids who qualify for the evaluation), so partially pooling is essential. 

Thanks to Stan, we've been able to construct reasonable estimates of the center-specific effects using Normal and t distributions for the center-level variation (the "random effect," though I know you hate that term); the estimates are close to each other, though it seems useful to allow for heavy tails.

After some prodding from our collaborators, we've recently started looking to DP priors for the center-level effects, especially after seeing these papers from Casella and co-authors. My questions:
  • What do you think of Dirichlet Process priors for something like this? I'm sure you've written about this (beyond BDA3), but I couldn't find much. I'm inclined to be very positive toward them, but I'm still new to this.
  • What do you think about trying to hack my way through this in Stan? I've loved having Stan for the rest of this project (in fact, I don't think the project would have been possible without Stan!), but I know that there's no pretty way to pull off a Dirichlet Process prior in Stan at the moment. Hence, before I abandon Stan for this part of the project, I figured it was worth asking.
Thanks, as always, for the help. And I'll be sending the current Head Start paper your way at some point soon.

- Avi
